claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) cause damage to DNA and proteins.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) cause damage to DNA and proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about oxidative stress.

claim: The RecA recombinase is oxidized by ROS.
source: Here, we report that the RecA recombinase is itself oxidized by ROS.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic and biochemical analyses, as well as mass spectrometry data showing RecA oxidation.

claim: Oxidation of RecA altered its DNA repair and DNA recombination activities.
source: Genetic and biochemical analyses revealed that oxidation of RecA altered its DNA repair and DNA recombination activities.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic and biochemical analyses demonstrating functional changes.

claim: Exposure to ROS converted four out of nine Met residues of RecA to methionine sulfoxide.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis showed that exposure to ROS converted four out of nine Met residues of RecA to methionine sulfoxide.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data is presented in the manuscript showing specific Met residue oxidation.

claim: Mimicking oxidation of Met35 by changing it for Gln caused complete loss of function.
source: Mimicking oxidation of Met35 by changing it for Gln caused complete loss of function
evidence: The manuscript presents data on RecAM35Q variant showing loss of function.

claim: Mimicking oxidation of Met164 resulted in constitutive SOS activation and loss of recombination activity.
source: mimicking oxidation of Met164 resulted in constitutive SOS activation and loss of recombination activity.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on RecAM164Q variant showing these phenotypes.

claim: All ROS-induced alterations of RecA activity were suppressed by methionine sulfoxide reductases MsrA and MsrB.
source: Yet, all ROS-induced alterations of RecA activity were suppressed by methionine sulfoxide reductases MsrA and MsrB.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic and biochemical data showing MsrA/B can restore RecA function.

claim: Under oxidative stress MsrA/B is needed for RecA homeostasis control.
source: These findings indicate that under oxidative stress MsrA/B is needed for RecA homeostasis control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Besides damaging DNA structure directly, ROS prevent repair of DNA damage by hampering RecA activity.
source: The implication is that, besides damaging DNA structure directly, ROS prevent repair of DNA damage by hampering RecA activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that RecA is oxidized and loses function under oxidative stress.

claim: Aerobic metabolism produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide (O2°-), hydroxyl radicals (HO°), and the non-radical molecule hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
source: Aerobic metabolism produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide (O2°-), hydroxyl radicals (HO°), and the non-radical molecule hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about aerobic metabolism.

claim: ROS arises from various external sources such as metal, UV radiation, or pathogen defenses.
source: Besides the endogenous production, ROS arises from various external sources such as metal, UV radiation, or pathogen defenses (Imlay, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Imlay, 2019.

claim: ROS are extremely harmful for the cell, leading to nucleic acid damages, protein oxidation, and lipid peroxidation.
source: ROS are extremely harmful for the cell, leading to nucleic acid damages, protein oxidation, and lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ROS effects.

claim: Exposure to ROS creates enough damage to impair cellular homeostasis in all living systems.
source: Exposure to ROS creates enough damage to impair cellular homeostasis in all living systems (Imlay, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Imlay, 2015.

claim: Within proteins, sulfur-containing cysteinyl and methionyl residues can be oxidized to sulfenic acid adducts and methionine sulfoxide, respectively.
source: Within proteins, sulfur-containing cysteinyl and methionyl residues can be oxidized to sulfenic acid adducts and methionine sulfoxide, respectively (Ezraty et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ezraty et al., 2017.

claim: Post-translational oxidations can be reversed by dedicated protein repair pathways present in all domains of life.
source: These post-translational oxidations can be reversed by dedicated protein repair pathways present in all domains of life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about protein repair systems.

claim: Thioredoxin/glutaredoxin reductases can reduce oxidized cysteinyl while methionine sulfoxide reductase (Msr) reduces methionine sulfoxide residues (Met-O).
source: Thioredoxin/glutaredoxin reductases can reduce oxidized cysteinyl while methionine sulfoxide reductase (Msr) reduces methionine sulfoxide residues (Met-O).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about protein repair enzymes.

claim: In prokaryotes, MsrA and MsrB are mostly present in the cytoplasm.
source: In prokaryotes, MsrA and MsrB are mostly present in the cytoplasm (Ezraty et al., 2017; Dos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ezraty et al., 2017 and Dos et al., 2018.

claim: MsrA and MsrB have a strict stereospecificity for their substrates, with MsrA reducing only Met-S-SO and MsrB reducing only Met-R-SO diastereoisomers.
source: MsrA and MsrB have a strict stereospecificity for their substrates, with MsrA reducing only Met-S-SO and MsrB reducing only Met-R-SO diastereoisomers.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MsrA and MsrB enzyme specificity.

claim: Full repair of a given cytosolic oxidized protein requires the action of both MsrA and MsrB.
source: Consequently, full repair of a given cytosolic oxidized protein requires the action of both MsrA and MsrB (Tsvetkov et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsvetkov et al., 2005.

claim: Lack of functional MsrA/B yielded to pleiotropic phenotypes related to bacterial virulence or aging.
source: Lack of functional MsrA/B yielded to pleiotropic phenotypes related to bacterial virulence or aging.
evidence: This is a general statement about known effects of MsrA/B deletion.

claim: Global proteomic or dedicated studies identified substrates, like the ubiquitous protein SRP54 and several other proteins listed in the database MetOSite.
source: Global proteomic or dedicated studies identified substrates, like the ubiquitous protein SRP54 (Ezraty et al., 2004; Gennaris et al., 2015) and several other proteins listed in the database MetOSite (https://metosite.uma.es) (Valverde et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RecA promotes DNA recombination and coordinates stress response by inducing the expression of the SOS regulatory system.
source: RecA promotes DNA recombination and coordinates stress response by inducing the expression of the SOS regulatory system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RecA function.

claim: RecA is targeted by ROS and this abrogates both RecA recombination and SOS induction capacities.
source: We report that RecA is targeted by ROS and this abrogates both RecA recombination and SOS induction capacities.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: MsrA/B are able to rescue oxidized RecA activities.
source: We show that MsrA/B are able to rescue oxidized RecA activities.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Met residues are not all oxidized at the same rate.
source: an in-depth analysis allowed us to show that Met residues are not all oxidized at the same rate
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing differential oxidation rates.

claim: Functional consequences of oxidation depend upon which Met residue is being hit.
source: functional consequences of oxidation depend upon which Met residue is being hit.
evidence: This is supported by data on different RecA variants with Met substitutions.

claim: Under oxidative stress both protein repair and de novo synthesis are used by Escherichia coli to replenish the pool of functional RecA above a threshold value.
source: Overall we discuss a model that predicts how under oxidative stress both protein repair and de novo synthesis are used by Escherichia coli to replenish the pool of functional RecA above a threshold value.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: An E. coli strain derivative lacking all peroxide-scavenging activities (catalases KatE and KatG, and peroxidase AhpC), referred to as Hpx-, accumulates micromolar amounts of H2O2.
source: An E. coli strain derivative lacking all peroxide-scavenging activities (catalases KatE and KatG, and peroxidase AhpC), referred to as Hpx-, accumulates micromolar amounts of H2O2 (Seaver and Imlay, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Seaver and Imlay, 2001.

claim: The Hpx- msrA msrB strain has significantly reduced viability upon UV stress compared to the Hpx- parental strain with around 1.4 log difference at 50 and 60 J/m2.
source: We found the Hpx- msrA msrB strain to have significantly reduced viability upon UV stress compared to the Hpx- parental strain with around 1.4 log difference at 50 and 60 J/m2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: UV defect is a hallmark of DNA recombination and/or repair defect.
source: UV defect is a hallmark of DNA recombination and/or repair defect.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about UV sensitivity.

claim: E. coli fights UV-induced DNA damages by both a RecA-dependent homologous recombination (HR) pathway and a RecA-independent UvrABCD-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.
source: E. coli fights UV-induced DNA damages by both a RecA-dependent homologous recombination (HR) pathway and a RecA-independent UvrABCD-dependent nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about E. coli DNA repair pathways.

claim: The recA mutation proved to be lethal in the Hpx- background in aerobic conditions.
source: In fact, the recA mutation proved to be lethal in the Hpx- background in aerobic conditions as previously reported (Park et al., 2005).
evidence: This observation is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2005.

claim: The Hpx- uvrA strain exhibited no phenotype, presumably because the HR pathway was sufficient to afford UV resistance.
source: In contrast, the Hpx- uvrA strain exhibited no phenotype, presumably because the HR pathway was sufficient to afford UV resistance.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The Hpx- msrA msrB uvrA strain showed hypersensitivity to O2, similar to the Hpx- recA strain.
source: The resulting Hpx- msrA msrB uvrA strain showed hypersensitivity to O2, similar to the Hpx- recA strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the presence of a higher-than-normal level of H2O2 RecA protein might be damaged by oxidation.
source: Altogether, these observations suggested that in the presence of a higher-than-normal level of H2O2 RecA protein might be damaged by oxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data presented.

claim: MsrA/B could be essential for maintaining a level of functional reduced RecA above a threshold value.
source: MsrA/B thus could be essential for maintaining a level of functional reduced RecA above a threshold value.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data presented.

claim: High recA gene dosage suppressed UV sensitivity of the Hpx msrA msrB mutant.
source: Consistently, we observed that high recA gene dosage suppressed UV sensitivity of the Hpx msrA msrB mutant (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High recA gene dosage suppressed the O2 sensitivity of the Hpx- msrA msrB uvrA.
source: and the O2 sensitivity of the Hpx- msrA msrB uvrA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RecA is a multifunctional protein serving in HR and SOS response regulation.
source: RecA is a multifunctional protein serving in HR and SOS response regulation (Clark and Margulies, 1965; Slilaty and Little, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Clark and Margulies, 1965 and Slilaty and Little, 1987.

claim: When using the Hpx- msrA msrB strain as a recipient, the transductant frequency dropped tenfold compared with the parental MsrA/B-proficient strain.
source: When using the Hpx- msrA msrB strain as a recipient, the transductant frequency dropped tenfold compared with the parental MsrA/B-proficient strain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transductant frequency was restored to the parental strain level by bringing in either plasmid-borne msrA or msrB genes.
source: Transductant frequency was restored to the parental strain level by bringing in either plasmid-borne msrA or msrB genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Hpx- strain exhibited enhanced SOS induction compared with the wild-type (WT) strain.
source: The Hpx- strain exhibited enhanced SOS induction compared with the wild-type (WT) strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Hpx- background has increased DNA damage level.
source: This was consistent with a previous work reporting increased DNA damage level in the Hpx- background (Courcelle et al., 2001; Mancini and Imlay, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Courcelle et al., 2001 and Mancini and Imlay, 2015.

claim: When msrA msrB deletions were introduced into the Hpx- background, the level of SOS induction decreased and was similar to that observed in the WT strain.
source: When msrA msrB deletions were introduced into the Hpx- background, the level of SOS induction decreased and was similar to that observed in the WT strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Hpx- strain exhibited an enhanced level of recA-gfp expression compared with the WT after MMC exposure.
source: The Hpx- strain exhibited an enhanced level of recA-gfp expression compared with the WT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deleting msrA msrB genes in the Hpx- strain impaired MMC induction of recA-gfp.
source: In contrast, deleting msrA msrB genes in the Hpx- strain impaired MMC induction of recA-gfp (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under oxidative stress MsrA/B maintains a level of reduced functional RecA necessary to carry out both efficient recombination and SOS regulation.
source: Altogether, these observations showed that under oxidative stress MsrA/B maintains a level of reduced functional RecA necessary to carry out both efficient recombination and SOS regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Purified RecA protein treated with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (50 mM) for 2 hr showed oxidation of four Met residues (Met35, Met58, Met164, and Met202) detectable by mass spectrometry.
source: First, purified RecA protein was treated with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (50 mM) for 2 hr and analyzed by mass spectrometry. On the nine Met residues present in RecA, four could be identified within peptides detectable by mass spectrometry after peptidase digestion.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Peptides containing Met28 and Met197 were too small to be detected by mass spectrometry.
source: In contrast, peptides containing Met28 and Met197 were too small to be detected.
evidence: This is a technical limitation noted in the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Met35, Met58, Met164, and Met202 were found to have around 20% of oxidation at baseline.
source: Likewise, Met35, Met58, Met164, and Met202 were found to have around 20% of oxidation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The basal level of oxidation could be explained by the use of in-gel digestion, a technique known to cause Met oxidation.
source: This basal level of oxidation could be explained by the use of in-gel digestion, a technique known to cause Met oxidation (Klont et al., 2018)
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Klont et al., 2018.

claim: After H2O2 treatment, the level of oxidation increased to approximately 90% at Met164- and Met202-containing positions.
source: After H2O2 treatment, the level of oxidation increased to approximately 90% at Met164- and Met202-containing positions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No Cys residue was found to be modified in RecA after H2O2 treatment.
source: Importantly, no Cys residue was found to be modified.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: RecA oxidized and then treated with MsrA/B enzymes in the presence of DTT showed a drastic decrease in its content of Met-O residues.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of RecArep revealed a drastic decrease in its content of Met-O residues (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RecA produced in a msrA msrB mutant exposed to HOCl treatment runs slower than RecA produced in a WT strain or in a msrA msrB mutant that has not been exposed to HOCl.
source: By western blot, we observed that RecA produced in a msrA msrB mutant exposed to HOCl treatment run slower than RecA produced in a WT strain or in a msrA msrB mutant that has not been exposed to HOCl (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RecA is subject to oxidation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: These results showed that RecA is subject to oxidation both in vitro and in vivo
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: In both in vitro and in vivo contexts MsrA/B allows reduction of Met-O residues present in RecAox.
source: and that in both contexts MsrA/B allows reduction of Met-O residues present in RecAox.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: RecA forms extended filaments on circular single strand (css) DNA in the presence of single-strand binding protein (SSB).
source: By using electron microscopy (Lusetti et al., 2003b), we observed that, in the presence of single-strand binding protein (SSB), RecA formed extended filaments on circular single strand (css) DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RecAox was unable to form extended filaments on cssDNA in the presence of SSB.
source: RecAox was unable to do so (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RecArep recovered part of its ability to form nucleoprotein filaments in the presence of SSB.
source: whereas RecArep recovered part of its ability to form nucleoprotein filaments in the presence of SSB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RecA exhibited DNA-dependent ATPase activity in the presence of SSB with an apparent kcat of 25.22 µM⋅min−1.
source: Using enzymatic assays, we showed that, as previously reported (Kowalczykowski and Krupp, 1987), RecA exhibited DNA-dependent ATPase activity in the presence of SSB with an apparent kcat of 25.22 µM⋅min−1.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data and a citation to Kowalczykowski and Krupp, 1987.

claim: RecAox was unable to hydrolyze ATP (SSB) with an apparent kcat of 0.26 µM⋅min−1.
source: In contrast, RecAox was unable to hydrolyze ATP (SSB) with an apparent kcat of 0.26 µM⋅min−1
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RecArep recovered a significant level of ATPase activity with an apparent kcat of 9.66 µM⋅min−1.
source: whereas RecArep recovered a significant level of activity with an apparent kcat of 9.66 µM⋅min−1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: RecA is known to promote DNA strand exchange.
source: RecA is also known to promote DNA strand exchange (Cox and Lehman, 1982; Lindsley and Cox, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cox and Lehman, 1982 and Lindsley and Cox, 1990.

claim: Formation of nicked circular product (N.P.) was observed in the RecA-containing sample but not in the RecAox-containing reaction.
source: Over time, formation of nicked circular product (N.P.) was observed in the RecA-containing sample but not in the RecAox-containing reaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA strand exchange assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RecArep was able to promote DNA strand exchange, though with reduced efficiency compared to RecA.
source: RecArep was also able to promote DNA strand exchange, though with reduced efficiency compared to RecA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA strand exchange assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RecAox protein cannot catalyze HR.
source: Together, our results show that RecAox protein cannot catalyze HR
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical assay data.

claim: MsrA/B is partially able to restore RecA HR activity.
source: which MsrA/B is partially able to restore.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical assay data.

claim: Met35 is located at the monomer–monomer interface in the RecA proto-filament.
source: Met35, which is targeted by oxidation, is located at the monomer–monomer interface in the RecA proto-filament (Figure 4A; McGrew and Knight, 2003; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citations to McGrew and Knight, 2003 and Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of RecAM35L and RecAM35Q variants was unable to rescue hypersensitivities of ∆recA and Hpx- ∆recA strains to MMC and O2, respectively.
source: Expression of RecAM35L and RecAM35Q variants was unable to rescue hypersensitivities of ∆recA and Hpx- ∆recA strains to MMC and O2, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The SOS response was abrogated in the ∆recA strain harboring RecAM35L and RecAM35Q.
source: Moreover, the SOS response was abrogated in the ∆recA strain harboring RecAM35L and RecAM35Q (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: RecAM35L variant had lost ATPase activity, nucleofilament formation, and DNA strand exchange capacities.
source: We performed biochemical analyses of the RecAM35L variant and found that it had lost ATPase activity, nucleofilament formation, and DNA strand exchange capacities (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Position 35 is functionally important, with little tolerance for substitution at this position.
source: Altogether, these studies indicated that position 35 is functionally important, with little tolerance for substitution at this position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on RecAM35L and RecAM35Q variants.

claim: The apparently essential role of Met35 was overlooked in previous multiple mutagenesis studies.
source: Surprisingly, such an apparently essential role of Met35 was overlooked in the previous multiple mutagenesis studies (McGrew and Knight, 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature supported by a citation to McGrew and Knight, 2003.

claim: Met164 is located in the L1 region that interacts with DNA.
source: Met164, identified above as a target of oxidation (Figure 3A), is located in the L1 region that interacts with DNA (Figure 4A; McGrew and Knight, 2003; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citations to McGrew and Knight, 2003 and Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of the RecAM164Q variant failed to complement hypersensitivity to MMC of ∆recA strain.
source: Expression of the RecAM164Q variant failed to complement hypersensitivity to MMC of ∆recA strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of the RecAM164L variant allowed full complementation of MMC hypersensitivity.
source: In contrast, expression of the RecAM164L variant allowed full complementation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Hpx- ∆recA strain was hypersensitive to O2 when expressing RecAM164Q but fully viable when expressing RecAM164L.
source: Similarly, the Hpx- ∆recA strain was hypersensitive to O2 when expressing RecAM164Q but fully viable when expressing RecAM164L (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A strain synthesizing RecAM164L exhibited WT-like features of MMC-induced SOS response.
source: A strain synthesizing RecAM164L exhibited WT-like features of MMC-induced SOS response within all tests listed above (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: A strain synthesizing RecAM164Q showed constitutive high levels of sfiA::lacZ expression, a high steady-state level of RecA, decreased levels of LexA, and strong cellular filamentation even in the absence of MMC.
source: Surprisingly, a strain synthesizing RecAM164Q showed constitutive high levels of sfiA::lacZ expression, a high steady-state level of RecA, decreased levels of LexA, and strong cellular filamentation even in the absence of MMC (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: The recA730 allele (RecAE38K) turns on the SOS response constitutively.
source: This phenotype was surprising and somehow echoed the long-studied recA730 allele (RecAE38K) as both alleles turn on the SOS response constitutively (Witkin et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Witkin et al., 1982.

claim: recA730 bears no phenotype regarding MMC sensitivity.
source: In contrast, recA730 bears no phenotype regarding MMC sensitivity (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The chromosomal recA-M164Q allele recapitulated all the phenotypes observed with a plasmid encoded RecAM164Q version.
source: The resulting strain recapitulated all the phenotypes observed with a plasmid encoded RecAM164Q version (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The recA-M164L containing strain showed a clear advantage over the WT strain under aerobic condition.
source: Under aerobic condition, the recA-M164L containing strain showed a clear advantage over the WT strain as, after a 120 hr growth, the population of the mutant counted for 70% of the total (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by competition assay data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Under anaerobic condition, both WT and recA-M164L strains grew at the same rate and a steady 50% ratio of both population was kept throughout the growth.
source: In contrast, under anaerobic condition, both strains grew at the same rate and a steady 50% ratio of both population was kept throughout the growth (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by competition assay data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Preventing oxidation of Met164 position provides E. coli with a better fitness.
source: This experiment showed that preventing oxidation of Met164 position provides E. coli with a better fitness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competition assay data.

claim: RecAM164Q produced normal-length nucleoprotein filaments in the absence of SSB, whereas RecAwt formed only short filaments.
source: Surprisingly, SSB was not required. In the absence of SSB, RecAM164Q produced normal-length nucleoprotein filaments, whereas RecAwt formed only short filaments (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: SSB was dispensable to facilitate ATPase activity of the RecAM164Q variant in the presence of cssDNA from M13 phage.
source: Next, enzymatic assays revealed that SSB was dispensable to facilitate ATPase activity of the RecAM164Q variant in the presence of cssDNA from M13 phage
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The apparent kcat of RecAM164Q was 21.75 µM⋅min−1 compared with the 10.78 µM⋅min−1 observed for the RecAwt.
source: and the apparent kcat of RecAM164Q was 21.75 µM⋅min−1 compared with the 10.78 µM⋅min−1 observed for the RecAwt (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The RecAM164Q variant displayed an enhanced filament propagation capacity, pointing to a potential hyper-reactivity of RecA toward ssDNA.
source: these observations indicated that the RecAM164Q variant displayed an enhanced filament propagation capacity, pointing to a potential hyper-reactivity of RecA toward ssDNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical data.

claim: The RecAM164Q variant binds cssDNA with the same affinity as RecA but fails to bind circular double strand (cds) nicked DNA.
source: Electrophoresis mobility shift assay (EMSA) techniques showed that the RecAM164Q variant binds cssDNA with the same affinity as RecA but fails to bind circular double strand (cds) nicked DNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changing Met164 for Q enables RecA to turn on the SOS response even in the absence of MMC-induced DNA damage.
source: These observations provided a molecular explanation as to why changing Met164 for Q, by inference oxidizing Met164 in Met-O, enabled RecA to turn on the SOS response even in the absence of MMC-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical data.

claim: The RecAM164Q variant was unable to initiate the DNA strand exchange, suggesting a defect in homologous pairing.
source: We observed that the RecAM164Q variant was unable to initiate the DNA strand exchange, suggesting a defect in homologous pairing (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA strand exchange assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The failure of the RecAM164Q variant to promote DNA strand exchange in vitro accounts for the in vivo hypersensitivity to MMC exposure of a strain synthesizing the RecAM164Q variant.
source: The failure of the variant to promote DNA strand exchange in vitro accounts for the in vivo hypersensitivity to MMC exposure of a strain synthesizing the RecAM164Q variant.
evidence: This is an inference connecting in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: Met58 proved to be totally resistant to oxidation.
source: Met58 proved to be totally resistant to oxidation (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Met58 is not solvent-exposed.
source: This is consistent with the fact it is not solvent-exposed.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge.

claim: Met202 was the more sensitive to oxidation.
source: Met202 was the more sensitive.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Mimetic oxidation variant RecAM202Q has been previously studied and shown to exhibit properties close to WT.
source: Interestingly, mimetic oxidation variant RecAM202Q has been previously studied (McGrew and Knight, 2003; Hörtnagel et al., 1999) and shown to exhibit properties close to WT
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McGrew and Knight, 2003 and Hörtnagel et al., 1999.

claim: Oxidation at Met202 position would bear no effect on RecA activity.
source: strongly supporting the notion that oxidation at that position would bear no effect on RecA activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies of RecAM202Q.

claim: Met164 was extremely sensitive to oxidation, although slightly less reactive than Met202, but far more sensitive than Met35.
source: Met164 was extremely sensitive as well, although slightly less reactive than Met202, but far more sensitive than Met35 (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Met residues are not equivalent in the face of a potent oxidative agent such as HOCl.
source: These results showed that Met residues are not equivalent in the face of a potent oxidative agent such as HOCl
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: M164 is highly prone to oxidation.
source: and that M164 is highly prone to oxidation.
